text: We've already seen how Larry, our leadership update agent, can access information, use tools, and ask for approval before taking action. But how do we decide which capabilities an agent actually needs, and how the work should be divided between the agent, automation, and people? That's what we need to establish before building, a clear sequence of work with the right responsibilities assigned to each part. To turn a workflow into a real agent, we can use our OVER framework to design the work. We start with the output we want, identify the verbs or individual steps required, evaluate which steps AI can handle, and route the work between AI, tools, and people. But designing the workflow is only half the challenge. We also need to turn that design into a system that can carry the work forward. Our agent-built blueprint brings the necessary capabilities together through five design decisions. First, the job. What exactly is the agent responsible for, and what does a successful result look like? Clear instructions establish that responsibility. Second, the knowledge. What information does the agent need? This includes relevant context and access to approved documents, data, or other sources. Third, the method. How should the work be performed? Instructions and reusable skills can establish consistent procedures for analyzing information, making comparisons, and checking results. Fourth, the capabilities. What does the agent need to do beyond generating a response? Connectors and tools let it retrieve information, interact with systems, and carry out actions. Finally, the control. How does the agent decide what happens next, and when should a human intervene? This is where orchestration comes in. The agent can select an available action, examine the result, and decide whether to continue or change course. It also needs to track its progress during the task and operate within clear permission, approval, and escalation boundaries. These five decisions give us a complete design without requiring unnecessary complexity. To put all this together, let's think back to Larry, our leadership update writer. His job is to produce a decision-ready leadership briefing. His knowledge comes from approved project information in SharePoint. His method is to identify meaningful developments, check important claims, and highlight decisions requiring attention. His capabilities allow him to retrieve information and prepare an update for Microsoft Teams. And his control allows him to investigate missing details, flag conflicting information, and request approval before publishing. Larry can now carry a meaningful multi-step workflow forward without us managing every action. The same blueprint works for any suitable workflow. Start with a clear job, give the agent what it needs, and retain human control where it matters. That's how we build agents that deliver real value without taking on more complexity than necessary.
